conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days, and it helps us figure out whether you might benefit from a little extra support right now.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team that cares for you—no judgment, just support. We’ll go one question at a own pace, and you can answer in your own words.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the last seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

It’s… it’s a little hard to explain. Some of the small things—like a hot cup of coffee in the morning or a song I used to love—still feel nice, but the spark is just… muted, I guess. I’m not completely numb, but I don’t get that lift I used to. It’s like I have to remind myself, “Hey, this should be making you happy,” instead of just feeling it naturally.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh, especially when my partner makes a goofy face at 3 a.m. during a diaper change, but it feels… thinner? Like the laugh comes out, but it doesn’t quite reach my belly the way it used to. Most of the time I’m too tired to even notice something’s funny, so when I do laugh it surprises me—like, “Oh, guess that was kind of funny,” instead of really feeling it first.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try—like when my mom says she’ll come hold the baby so I can take a walk, I tell myself I *should* be excited about that. But the second I imagine it, this wave of “meh” hits. I still go, and once I’m outside I can notice the air feels nice, but the looking-forward part barely shows up. Even little milestones—baby’s first real bath, getting a pumpkin-spice latte again—sound good in theory, yet I don’t feel that buzz of anticipation. It’s more like I’m checking off “fun” things I’m supposed to do rather than actually craving them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that, mostly over tiny stuff. Yesterday he spit up right after I’d changed him and I thought, “Great, I must’ve jostled him too much.” Or if he’s fussy and I can’t settle him, I’ll assume it’s because I’m not doing the right swaddle or I ate something weird. I know, logically, babies just spit up and cry, but in the moment it feels like I should have prevented it. It’s not constant—more like quick jabs of “this is my fault,” and then I try to shake it off.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just starts racing out of nowhere, even when the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet. I’ll lie there checking the monitor every few minutes, convinced something’s wrong even though he’s fine. And when we’re out walking, I worry the stroller sunshade isn’t shading enough, or that someone’s going to cough near him. I know it’s not rational, but I can’t shake the “what-if” loop in my head until we’re back home.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice this week I’ve had that sudden wave—like I’m standing on the edge of something, even if I’m just folding laundry. My chest gets tight, everything feels too bright or too loud, and for a minute I think, “What if I drop him? What if I can’t breathe?” It passes pretty quickly, especially if I can sit and take a few slow breaths, but those flashes come out of nowhere and leave me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the second I finish one thing, three more pop up. I’ll finally get him down for a nap, realize I haven’t eaten, then notice the sink’s full of bottles, and suddenly I’m standing in the kitchen holding a cold piece of toast, not sure which task to tackle next. I’m not falling apart, but there’s this constant background hum of “I’m behind,” and by evening I’m just wiped—like I’ve been paddling hard to keep my head above water all day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but several nights this week I’ve lain there wired even when the baby’s out cold. My mind just keeps looping—did I sterilize the pump parts, is he breathing, what if I oversleep the next feed… I’m not sobbing or anything, just can’t shut it off. I’ll finally drift off, then every squeak from the bassinet jolts me awake. By morning I feel like I’ve been lightly dozing instead of really sleeping.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get hit with that some evenings—this heavy, blah feeling that settles in my chest. It’s not all day, but when it shows up I just feel… flat, like the color’s drained out of the room. I might tear up a little watching some silly commercial, or when a lullaby comes on. The sadness isn’t crushing, more like a dull ache that reminds me I’m not myself right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really—no full-on crying spells. A couple of times my eyes have welled up when I couldn’t get him settled and felt totally spent, but the tears never actually roll. It’s more like I get that tight throat and blink a lot, then swallow hard and keep rocking him. So, no, I haven’t cried, just felt on the verge once or twice.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or low, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared that the joy in everyday moments feels muted and that looking forward to things you once anticipated feels more like a chore. Even laughter seems "thinner," and evenings bring a dull, heavy sadness that lingers. Anxious thoughts loop about the baby's safety, and sudden waves of panic leave you shaky and breathless. You're coping day-to-day but feel constantly behind and exhausted by bedtime. You're not having thoughts of self-harm-your focus is on wanting to feel like yourself again so you can care for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-total loss of anticipatory joy, even for events she believes she "should" be excited about; this aligns with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges blaming herself "some of the time" over minor infant issues, fitting "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, and uncontrollable anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart) and persistent 'what-if' worries, matching 'Yes, very often.</sym>, <sym>She describes sudden, unexpected episodes of intense anxiety (chest tightness, sensory overload, intrusive catastrophic thoughts) happening multiple times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty keeping up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports difficulty sleeping on several nights, racing thoughts, and frequent awakenings, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences noticeable, recurrent evening sadness with tearfulness and anhedonia—semantically aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 19 on the EPDS meets the threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. The patient describes persistent loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), recurrent sadness, self-blame, racing heart and panic episodes, and difficulty sleeping unrelated to infant care. These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 is negative, indicating no current self-harm risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or perinatal mental-health service for full assessment
2. Share EPDS results and request discussion of therapy options such as <med>CBT</med> or medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Ask about local mother-infant support groups and peer programs for new moms
4. Practice brief breathing exercises when panic sensations arise; keep sessions short and baby-safe
5. Prioritize rest by accepting help with night feeds or household tasks whenever possible
6. Schedule routine follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor symptom trend
7. If mood worsens, thoughts of harm emerge, or panic escalates, contact your provider immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wks PP

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in anticipatory pleasure; laughter described as “thinner”  
- Low mood: intermittent “heavy, blah” feeling, color “drained,” tearfulness without full crying spells  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame over minor infant issues  
- Anxiety: persistent “what-if” rumination, racing heart, situational panic (tight chest, sensory overload)  
- Overwhelm: constant sense of “behind,” multiple tasks “on top of me”  
- Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep unrelated to infant needs  
- No anhedonia or sadness present all day; no self-harm ideation

**Pattern**  
Mixed anxious-depressive presentation: mood lability, guilt, and anxious hypervigilance predominate; functional impact moderate (able to complete care tasks but reports “wiped”).

**Screening significance**  
EPDS equivalent items: #1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, #7, #8 positive; #9, #10 negative.  
Meets provisional cut-off for probable postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety; safety risk absent.

**Risk factors noted**  
- Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, self-criticism, somatic anxiety, no social withdrawal reported.

**Observation**  
Patient demonstrates good insight, no psychotic or self-harm features; appropriate bonding statements; warrants further clinical evaluation and monitoring for symptom escalation.
